newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal union seeks 32-hour working week.
newsitem.headline: German metal union seeks 32-hour working week.

text.p: Germany's largest trade union, the metalworkers' union IG Metall said this week it would push hard to cut the working week to 32 hours in forthcoming pay talks, to help remedy Germany's chronic jobless problem.

Klaus Zwickel, IG Metall's chairman, also said the union would not be adopting measures agreed by chemical-workers' union IG Chemie, which offers employers an "out" clause on existing wage pacts if hard times look like closing a firm.
"We cannot stop the rise in unemployment without massive cuts in the working week," Zwickel said, as he called for wide-scale support from the opposition Social Democratics (SPD) and the Greens.

Germany's once-admired system of thrashing out a consensus between employers and unions on wage pacts is close to buckling under the strain of record unemployment, which reached an unadjusted total of 4.25 million in April.
Employers are also looking for ways to boost Germany's international competitiveness and see increased flexibility from the workers as a useful place to start.

IG Metall, which has nearly three million members, is preparing for a tough round of horse trading on the thorny issue of the shorter working week when preliminary wage negotiations for 1999 kick off in late 1998.

Even within the union itself it is undecided whether or not the union should go all-out to bring in the shorter week, which would involve a 32-hour week in western Germany and a 35-hour week in the east.

There were disagreements between Zwickel and the deputy chairman Walter Riester, on whether the working week should be shortened generally or via a bundle of measures, including reduced overtime or through special measures for shift workers or part-time workers.

Any wage cuts relating to a cut in the working week would depend on the effect the shorter week had on the jobs market, but a graded, differentiated pay settlement would be the best solution, Zwickel said.
Lower income groups would keep full pay, while those in medium and higher income brackets would receive comparatively less in a settlement.
Zwickel said he believes that Labour coming to power in Britain and the Socialist victory in France had improved the prospects for a shorter working week across Europe.

While other unions have said that they would be interested in following the example set by the chemical union agreement allowing for out clauses in cases of extreme economic hardship, Zwickel was sceptical.

He said that such clauses already existed in the metal industry and he knew of no cases where a company had been in danger of being closed and the unions had not given its agreement to an exceptional clause to save the company.
However, he said it was possible that individual firms would use the opt-out clause to gain competitive edge against their rivals, which could undermine the whole pay talk structure.
The unions offered the employers further talks on the issue, while the employers in the German state of Hesse said that the idea of a 32-hour week was absurd.

IG Metall would discuss the proposal until the end of 1998, when the wages commission would decide whether the 32-hour working week could be proposed at the wage talks. --Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525
